title: Industry Pulse — AI / Agent Ecosystem

bullets.title: The MCP 2026-07-28 spec is final and stateless — sessions, the initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone, and Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated
bullets.summary: The final spec removes the initialize / notifications/initialized handshake entirely; every request now carries its protocol version and client capabilities inline in _meta (io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities). Sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header are removed from the Streamable HTTP transport, so a remote server that previously needed sticky sessions and a shared session store can now sit behind a plain round-robin load balancer, route on an Mcp-Method header, and let clients cache tools/list for as long as the server's ttlMs permits. Roots, Sampling and Logging remain functional but are deprecated — new implementations should not add them. A ten-week validation window from the July 28 ship date puts the Tier 1 SDK deadline at roughly October 6.
bullets.how: This is a deliberate backfill, not a fresh headline, and it is exactly the item yesterday's PRAXIS lesson said we were structurally blind to: a dated migration deadline that no single day reports as news. The Construct runs on MCP servers across Slack, Gmail, Drive, Higgsfield, Canva, Quartr and a dozen others, plus whatever we author ourselves — and every one of them has a clock on it now. Three concrete moves. First, this is the founding entry in the deprecation calendar we said we needed: endpoint, end-of-life, migration owner, with MCP's ~Oct 6 SDK window as the first line item. Second, any MCP server we write ourselves must be authored stateless-first from today — building on sessions now is building on a removed feature. Third, the deprecation of Sampling matters specifically to us: any agent design that assumed a server could call back into the model needs a different shape, and it is cheaper to find that now than in October.

bullets.title: Claude Code 2.1.234 ships GitLab merge-request support in the statusline and, more importantly for us, stronger gateway and plugin validation
bullets.summary: Released Aug 17. The visible additions are an optional CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME environment variable, a selection:clear keybinding action, and a GitLab merge-request badge in the footer and statusline. The less-advertised changes are faster self-hosted runner starts, tightened gateway and plugin validation, and a batch of fixes across Linux, Windows, MCP, permissions and session handling.
bullets.how: The GitLab badge is irrelevant to us; the plugin validation is not. The Construct runs a large installed-skills and plugin surface, and tightened validation is the kind of change that silently rejects a plugin that used to load — the failure mode is an agent quietly missing a capability, not an error we would notice. Worth a pass over the plugin fleet to confirm everything still registers after the update. Faster self-hosted runner starts is the one with real leverage if we ever move the ANS engine queue or the Mallard cron onto self-hosted runners.

bullets.title: Japan and South Korea move in opposite directions on AI training data on the same day — Tokyo toward forced disclosure, Seoul toward consent-free training
bullets.summary: South Korea is advancing a Personal Information Protection Act amendment that would, for the first time, let controllers use original non-pseudonymized personal data for AI development without the data subject's consent and beyond the original purpose of collection, provided the Personal Information Protection Commission approves and basic security standards are met — regulator-gated rather than rule-gated. In the same window Japan's cabinet is preparing transparency rules that would force developers to disclose training inputs and processing methods, aimed at preventing IP theft. Both sit against the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations, enforceable since Aug 2.
bullets.how: No operational impact on B9 or the fleet today; neither jurisdiction is a market we serve. The reason it earns a slot is that it is the second consecutive day where the significant item arrived as policy rather than as a launch, and it sharpens the PRAGMA angle from yesterday's watermarking bullet. The emerging shape is that AI provenance and disclosure obligations are fragmenting by jurisdiction faster than any vendor's compliance posture can track, and a client operating across markets now has a real question — what is disclosed, where, and by whom — that nobody is answering for them. That is a consulting surface adjacent to what PRAGMA already sells, and it is worth watching rather than acting on.

bullets.title: Perplexity's Agent API keeps absorbing third-party frontier models — grok-4.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning are now callable through one orchestration endpoint
bullets.summary: Perplexity's Agent API, part of the platform expansion alongside the Embeddings and Sandbox APIs, has added support through its August changelog for xAI's xai/grok-4.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (a 1M-token-context open reasoning model) and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, on top of existing OpenAI and Claude routing plus live web search and reasoning controls. Individual entries are dated across the month rather than to a single announcement, so treat this as a trend line, not an Aug 18 event.
bullets.how: Read this next to Monday's Stripe-OpenRouter item and the pattern is unmistakable: the orchestration layer is consolidating, and every serious player is racing to become the single endpoint in front of everyone else's models. For The Construct the practical implication is unchanged and now doubly reinforced — keep every gateway behind our own thin adapter, because the number of parties who would like to own our routing is growing, not shrinking. The narrower opportunity is that a single endpoint carrying grok-4.6, DeepSeek and Claude is a cheap way to run genuine cross-model comparisons for the PRAGMA Mirror brand-visibility scan without maintaining four separate integrations — worth a spike, not a migration.

praxis_lesson: Today's 24-hour window contained almost no launches — the Claude Code point release was the only genuine same-day platform item — and the honest read is that a scan tuned exclusively to new announcements would have returned nearly nothing. The value today came entirely from executing yesterday's lesson rather than from fresh news: the MCP stateless spec has been final since July 28 with a migration deadline around October 6, and it never entered this report because no single day treated it as news. That is the whole argument for the deprecation calendar in one item. So the operating change is to stop measuring this scan by how much is new and start measuring it by how much is due — a slow week is precisely when the backfill sweep over deadlines, deprecations and policy earns its keep, because those items never announce themselves and they are the ones that break production. Second observation, minor but real: two days running, the most strategically significant item arrived as regulation rather than as a product, which suggests the provenance-and-disclosure thread deserves a standing watch rather than opportunistic coverage.
